The croft sits above a quay shed, its shutters nailed shut on the river side. I know the berth by its stair: fourteen treads, the ninth one soft, the top landing eight feet long. I time the last approach by the piles. A groan, then twelve counts, then the lamp's hiss rising through the boards below me. I climb on the groan. The soft tread gives under my heel, and I step over it.

Inside, the air is cold and smells of lamp oil and old paper. A plank rests across two sawhorses under the window, its surface scored with the marks of other surveys. I lay my steel rule along the far edge and set the lamp at its end, turned to a bead. Folio two hundred and fourteen lies flat against my ribs. I take it out and set it on the plank. The strip and the tag come out of my palm and sit beside it.

I weight the corners with the rule's ends, the bone edge pressed square to the grain. Then I test the spine. I run my thumbnail along the stitching, slow, and feel for give. It is sound. Someone sewed this folio with care.

Breathe. Count four. Count four again. My fingers are steady now, and I keep them that way.

I turn the first leaf with my thumb's edge. The paper rasps, dry and exact. I count as I go. Sixteen sheets to the gathering, and the gatherings stack against my thumb like plates. Two hundred and fourteen leaves, or near it. The waxed thread tracer is still knotted at the gutter, one loop pulled tight. I leave it where it is.

The first entries are shipping lists in a clerk's square hand. Barrel staves. Canvas bales. Tallow, weighed in hundredweights. Each line carries a time, struck in the margin: a bell-hour, a quarter past. Then the coded marks begin. A crate number with a bracket. Two initials, always the same pair, set beside sums that do not match the manifests. Then the same line again, in another folio, cross-referenced back to this one.

QY-A7 appears on the eleventh leaf, written three times in one column. The first is an arrival. The second is a departure. The third has no time at all, only the designation and a small tick, the same tick I saw beside the entry in the ledgeryard.

Then the margin note, in the hard-pressed hand. *Channel rerouted — covert quay suspected.* It is written on the same page as a payment. The sum is entered under a ward, then struck through, then entered again under a second ward a little further down the river.

I mark the bearings. Who: the initials, repeated, a hand that signs its own ticks. When: the times against the lighter's crests, the tide-hours in the margins. Where: QY-A7, moving from one channel to another, the river bent to hide it. The benefit runs one way. Whoever holds that water holds what passes through it, and whoever pays for the ward moves the money after the water.

My jaw sets. I notice it only because my teeth ache. I do not let my hand shake.

I tear a scrap of cream paper from the strip, no larger than a thumbnail. On it I write one figure in pencil: *11*, the leaf where QY-A7 sits three times. I fold the scrap twice and tuck it into the folio's gutter, flush with the thread, so the number faces the spine. Then I take the last of the waxed thread from my coat and tie a single knot to the spine stitch, tight, not showing from the front. If anyone opens the folio and does not know to look, they will not find it. If they do, they will know I was here.

Last, I close the cover. I press the folio flat under the rule and sit with my palm on its face for one long breath.

The lamp hisses. I lift my thumbnail to the plank's edge and drive a scratch into the wood, a datum, small and square. Under the window the piles give, a long groan through the joists, and I feel it in my spine. I hold my thumb to the wood until the sound is gone.

Then I slide the folio back against my ribs, where it will be warm, and wipe the pencil from my palm with my sleeve, leaving only the number *214* pressed into the skin.

I stay in the eaves' shadow and count the lane's length by its stones. Eleven paces to the bollard. Six along the wall. At the hook above the water stair, where a rope is belayed to an iron ring, I stop and lay two fingers on the rope's lay.

Renn's tracer sits there, a loop of waxed thread drawn round the hook and cinched flat. Its knot is a single turn and a tuck, pulled so tight the tar on the rope has softened under it and hardened again. The loose end runs off the hook toward the bridge, no thicker than a hair, lying along the wall's mortar where a hand would not catch it. I follow it with my thumbnail. The thread is cold and taut. It does not sag.

I run the rule along the thread's line, lightly, until its bone edge touches the mortar seam. The line leads north and west, past the drain grate, along the lower wall to the bridge's foot. I keep my rule at my wrist and walk the thread the way I would walk a chain.

The lamp at the bridge hisses through its crack. Under the planks, the piles groan, and the span takes the weight and gives back a finger's width. I wait for the groan to finish, then set my heel on the first plank. It rings a little, then holds. I step where the thread lies, and no farther.

At the post, the nail head is where I left it. The seam beside it is a hair wider on the left. The thread runs down into it and stops.

I lay the blade's flat into the seam and ease the plank a fraction. Beneath it the stringer is cold. Above me on the rail's cap, the folio lies in its place, squared to the grain, though I cannot see it. I feel for its last leaf with the tips of two fingers. The scrap is there, folded twice, its fold pressed flat, the waxed loop drawn through the stitch.

A barge horn sounds from the mouth, short. A wash rolls under the span and lifts the planks, and the thread jumps against my finger. I stop. One breath. Two. The wake drops. The planks settle.

I slide my thumb under the scrap's fold. The edge is cool. I ease the loop back through the stitch a hair at a time, feeling the give, and the thread slips free without a snap. I draw the scrap out flat with the blade's point and close my hand around it.

I unfold the scrap in my palm and read it by touch. My own figure, small and square, the corrected digit. Beside it, faint, Vesh's thumb has left its shine. He has read it. He has accepted it.

The chill of the rule edge bites my wrist as I set it down. The coin's nick is warm under my thumb.

I slide the folded scrap back under the leaf with my thumbnail, pressing its fold flat, and the new tracer slides into the seam. The lamp hisses through its crack. The piles groan beneath the span, long and low, and the planks give under my heel and hold.
